Getting Started

This tutorial walks through building a SNGL app from a one-line Hello World up to a full todo list, then shows how to embed the generated code in a larger project.

Hello, World

A SNGL app is one or more windows, each the root of a tree of components. The smallest app is a window holding a single text node:

import "sngl:ui"

ui.window(title="Hello") {
    ui.text(value="Hello, World!")
}

import "sngl:ui" brings in the UI library under the name ui. Save the file as hello.sngl and run it in a browser:

sngl run hello.sngl --platform html

Reactive state and binding

State is declared with var (mutable) or a zero-argument func (derived). The :value prefix on a prop is two-way binding: changes flow both ways. Replace the contents of hello.sngl with:

import "sngl:ui"

ui.window(title="Hello") {
    var name = "World"
    func greeting() => "Hello, {name}!"
    ui.vbox(style={gap=8px, padding=16px}) {
        ui.text(value=greeting)
        ui.input(:value=name)
    }
}

When the user types in the input, name updates, greeting recomputes, and the text re-renders. No subscriptions to wire up. value=greeting names the function without calling it: a zero-argument function is called wherever its value is read, so the prop always shows the current greeting.

Run it on any platform

Pick a target. The same source compiles to all of them. The first run of a Go target downloads and compiles its dependencies, which can take several minutes with no output; later runs start in seconds.

Generate code you can wrap

sngl run is for iteration. To produce source you can ship inside a larger project, use sngl generate, which writes the code to a directory (-o) and stops. Each target's options, passed as --opt key=value, are listed on its page under Platforms. Pick a target:

Pre-configure with output

Repeating --lang and --platform flags is tedious. An output block in the source declares the targets up front; bare sngl run and sngl generate then pick them up automatically. It goes at the top level of the file, beside the window, and a package has at most one.

output {
    none { html }
    go {
        bubbletea
        fyne
    }
    kotlin { android }
}

Each language–platform pair in the block becomes one build. none is the language for a target that needs no host language, which is what a static page is. Same source, four outputs.

sngl generate writes every build into the current directory, or into -o. sngl run runs the builds one after another in the order listed, each starting when the one before exits; a served page never exits, and Ctrl-C stops sngl run altogether, so pass --platform to run just one. The flags still win over the block: sngl generate --platform bubbletea builds only that pair.

Build a todo app

Now the full thing: a list of todos with an input field, an add button, and a checkbox per item. Save it as todo.sngl; every line is part of the running app, and the paragraphs after it explain the pieces.

import "sngl:ui"

struct Todo {
    text string = ""
    done bool = false
}

ui.window(title="Todos") {
    var (
        newTodo = ""
        todos list[Todo] = []
    )
    func status() => "Todo List ({todos.length} items)"

    ui.vbox(style={gap=12px, padding=16px}) {
        ui.text(value=status, style={fontWeight=bold, fontSize=24px})
        ui.hbox(style={gap=8px, alignItems=center}) {
            ui.input(:value=newTodo, placeholder="Buy eggs", style={flex=1})
            ui.button(text="Add", @click {
                todos.push(Todo{text=newTodo})
                newTodo = ""
            })
        }
        ui.vbox(style={gap=4px}) {
            for var &item = todos {
                ui.checkbox(:checked=item.done, label=item.text)
            } else {
                ui.text(value="Nothing to do.", style={color=#888888})
            }
        }
    }
}

struct Todo is the data shape. var todos list[Todo] = [] starts empty and is what the UI iterates. func status() is derived — the count updates whenever todos changes. The state is scoped to the window's body; nothing outside it can touch it.

@click is an event handler running a statement block; todos.push(...) mutates the list, which updates what is rendered. for var &item binds each element by reference, so the checkbox's :checked binding writes straight back into the list. The loop's else renders when the list is empty.

Persist state with a Go import

The todo list lives in memory. To save it across runs, import a Go package: its exported functions become SNGL functions with the same signature, and its exported types become SNGL types.

A go: import resolves through the Go module in the current directory, so make the directory holding todo.sngl a module and put the package in it:

go.mod           module myapp
store/store.go
todo.sngl
package store

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"os"
)

type Todo struct {
	Text string
	Done bool
}

const file = "todos.json"

func Load() []Todo {
	var todos []Todo
	if b, err := os.ReadFile(file); err == nil {
		json.Unmarshal(b, &todos)
	}
	return todos
}

func Save(todos []Todo) {
	if b, err := json.Marshal(todos); err == nil {
		os.WriteFile(file, b, 0o644)
	}
}

The list now holds the Go package's Todo rather than one declared in SNGL, since that is the type Load returns and Save takes. Its fields keep their Go names with the first letter lowercased: Text is text.

import "go:myapp/store"
import "sngl:ui"

ui.window(title="Todos") {
    var newTodo = ""
    var todos list[store.Todo] = store.Load()

    effect(on=todos, @update(t) {
        store.Save(t)
    })

    ui.vbox(style={gap=12px, padding=16px}) {
        ui.hbox(style={gap=8px, alignItems=center}) {
            ui.input(:value=newTodo, placeholder="Buy eggs", style={flex=1})
            ui.button(text="Add", @click {
                todos.push(store.Todo{text=newTodo})
                newTodo = ""
            })
        }
        for var &item = todos {
            ui.checkbox(:checked=item.done, label=item.text)
        }
    }
}

An effect keyed on todos reports every write to it: @update runs after the handler that wrote it -- the push, a checkbox toggling an item, a replacement -- and is handed the list as it now is. So store.Load and store.Save are ordinary calls at the two ends of its life. A go: import compiles only for a Go target; on another target, use a persistence package for that platform.
